practicalQuestion: When symptoms and clinic-based measures have normalized but high-speed and sport-specific exposure remain incomplete, how should physical therapy and performance staff structure the next 7–10 days and define progress, hold, or regress criteria without relying on a single return-to-sport cutoff?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete nearing unrestricted participation after a lower-extremity injury
decisionContext.sport: Field sport with sprinting, cutting, and reactive demands
decisionContext.phase: Modified participation to unrestricted team activity
decisionContext.outcome: Coordinate staged exposure and decision ownership across rehabilitation and performance staff
decisionContext.constraints: Limited practice opportunities; competition schedule continues; no athlete-identifying or diagnosis-specific data

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests how to structure a 7 to 10 day bridge from modified to unrestricted participation, or tests progress, hold, or regress rules. The relevant evidence is indirect. It comes from one large on-field rehabilitation case series and one single-athlete case study after ACL reconstruction in male soccer, a small case series of elite sprinters with hamstring strains, a survey of physical therapists, and observational load studies in professional soccer squads in regular in-season training. These sources agree that controlled rehabilitation work falls short of match demands, especially for decelerations and other high-intensity mechanical actions. They also show tension between common strength-based release criteria and athlete readiness. The sprint exposure evidence is weak: the two-days-before-match finding rests on zero injuries with overlapping confidence intervals and no pooled difference, and the strength study used a different speed threshold and did not measure injury.

dimensions.sourceReview: Every claim is checked against original source text. Designs are case series, a single-case study, a practitioner survey, and retrospective or prospective observational cohorts. There are no controlled trials of return-to-sport progression.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. Sources describe on-field rehabilitation loads, criteria in use, and sprint exposure patterns in uninjured squads. None tests a short end-stage progression plan or decision rules.
dimensions.consistency: Consistent that controlled rehabilitation work stays below match demands and that single strength cutoffs are not enough. Sprint exposure findings use different thresholds and outcomes and do not resolve dosing for a returning athlete.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. Studied groups are male professional or amateur soccer players, elite sprinters, and Brazilian elite club physical therapists. None are collegiate field-sport athletes, and two key sources are specific to ACL reconstruction or hamstring strain.

bottomLine.text: The library does not test a specific 7 to 10 day plan or progress, hold, or regress rules. Indirect evidence suggests that controlled on-field rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction approached team-training volumes but fell short on deceleration and peak speed and stayed well below match demands, so further modified training before full team integration was recommended. Strength and flexibility above 90% of the uninjured leg did not match sprinters' own readiness for maximal speed, and case authors stress parallel collaboration between rehabilitation and performance staff. Treat any plan as a staff-designed option set, not an evidence-tested protocol.

actions.title: Option: close specific gaps toward team-training, then match-like outputs
actions.text: In 100 male soccer players after ACL reconstruction, only a third reached the final on-field stage. In that stage, total, high-intensity, and acceleration distance matched or exceeded team-training values, but peak speed reached 88% and deceleration distance 48% of team training, and all outputs stayed well below match values. The authors conclude players were underprepared for deceleration demands and that on-field rehabilitation does not fully prepare players for full team training, so further modified training is needed. In a single elite case, peak running intensity could match the player's own pre-injury team training and match values, but mechanical work per minute could not, and the authors state only small-sided games with few players (3v3 or 4v4) are effective for that. In the return-to-train phase, the case team used partial team sessions, such as joining only some drills or playing small-sided games as a floater. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): use the remaining days to close specific gaps, such as decelerations and reactive cutting, through partial team drills rather than adding total distance, and set the daily sequence locally.

actions.title: Option: plan near-maximal speed exposures inside the microcycle
actions.text: In elite teams in regular in-season training, not athletes returning from injury, there were no match hamstring injuries in 480 player-turnarounds when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed occurred two days before a match. However, confidence intervals overlapped, the pooled analysis showed no difference in injury rate with versus without exposure, and the authors state the design precludes causal conclusions and that false positives are possible. They suggest these exposures may concern the whole squad only in 6 to 8 day turnarounds and only substitutes in 3 to 5 day turnarounds, and that the days before be tailored so players do not arrive fatigued. In 58 professional male players who averaged about one effort per week, weeks with 7 to 8 efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were associated with very small drops in eccentric hamstring strength, and injury was not measured. In one reserve squad, players with no match time still accumulated about one match's worth of weekly high-speed and sprint distance, half that of 90-minute players. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): schedule a small number of near-maximal exposures with recovery around them and check the strength and symptom response. These are associations in uninjured players, not limits or targets for a returning athlete.

actions.title: Option: use a panel of criteria instead of one cutoff
actions.text: In 18 elite sprinters, strength and flexibility above 90% of the uninjured leg at 6 weeks did not match the sprinters' own readiness for maximal speed. Surveyed physical therapists most often progressed rehabilitation on pain, strength, and function, and released athletes to team training or transition staff mainly on strength (71%) and sprint or high-speed running performance (58%), with 32% using GPS external load. The survey authors note progression criteria are not consistent in the literature, and they cite an expert consensus listing medical staff clearance, pain-free testing, similar flexibility, field-test performance, and psychological readiness. In the ACL case series, stage transitions combined how the knee and soft tissues responded to loads with defined stage-specific criteria. In the single case, step impulse asymmetry with knee pain on return to running led to a few days without running, and both resolved on a softer pitch. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): progress when clinic, field, and readiness signals agree, hold when one domain lags, and regress when symptoms, asymmetry, or field outputs worsen.

actions.title: Option: name decision owners for each step
actions.text: Citing earlier work, the case series authors describe on-field rehabilitation as the bridge between clinic-managed rehabilitation and the team-training environment with coaching and performance staff. The single-case authors stress continuous and parallel collaboration within the multidisciplinary team, even when late conditioning looks performance-staff led. The survey authors suggest that in some clubs strength and conditioning coaches may be in charge of the transition to the field. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): agree in advance who sets daily loads, who reviews field and clinical data, and who makes progression and clearance calls.

monitoring.label: Field outputs against the athlete's own references
monitoring.text: Track high-intensity distance, peak speed, accelerations, and decelerations. The single-case authors compared rehabilitation peaks with the player's own pre-injury team training and match data and recommend collecting such reference points during the season, while the case series lacked pre-injury peak speed data for most players. In the case series, total distance plateaued and the authors suggest it is not useful for return-to-competition decisions or for progressing through on-field stages, and deceleration distance lagged most.

monitoring.label: Stride and step impulse asymmetry
monitoring.text: Case study authors report that GPS-embedded inertial sensors can monitor stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries to guide phase progression. In that case, an asymmetry with knee pain on return to running led to a few days off running. This was one elite case, not a validated decision tool.

monitoring.label: Strength response to high-speed exposure
monitoring.text: If eccentric hamstring testing is available, review it alongside weekly near-maximal efforts. In professional players who averaged about one such effort per week, weeks with 7 to 8 efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were linked to very small strength decreases. The study did not measure injury.

monitoring.label: Athlete-reported readiness
monitoring.text: Ask the athlete about readiness for maximal speed. In elite sprinters, strength and flexibility above 90% of the uninjured leg did not match their own judgment of readiness.

guardrails.text: Progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians. The cited expert consensus lists medical staff clearance as a criterion, and this brief does not clear an athlete or set policy.

Do not use sprint exposure numbers as fixed limits or targets. They come from observational studies of uninjured professional soccer players, the two-days-before-match finding had overlapping confidence intervals and no pooled difference, and the strength study did not measure injury.

Injury-specific benchmarks should not be applied without clinician input because the diagnosis here is not specified. After a hamstring graft, the case team used strength benchmarks such as above 90% eccentric strength before near-maximal speeds, and, citing earlier work, the authors call hamstring strength an important but not unique criterion for speed progression.

limitations.text: The on-field evidence is a case series of 100 male soccer players and a single elite male case after ACL reconstruction, with no control group. The five-stage framework used is based on expert opinion, and the case series authors say it is unclear whether higher return rates in players reaching the final stage were caused by the workloads.
Sprint exposure and match-time load findings come from squads in regular in-season training, not athletes in a return phase, and are observational. The strength study did not measure injury.

Criteria evidence comes from 18 elite sprinters and a survey of Brazilian elite club physical therapists. The survey authors note that the predictive value and cut-offs of these criteria still need study.

whatCouldChange.text: Validated cut-offs that predict reinjury after return, which the survey authors say are still lacking.

evidenceTension.text: Surveyed physical therapists most often used muscle strength as a release criterion, but in elite sprinters strength and flexibility above 90% of the uninjured leg did not match readiness to sprint at maximal speed. Separately, exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed two days before a match were followed by no match hamstring injuries in elite squads, though confidence intervals overlapped and the pooled analysis showed no difference. In a different squad, 7 to 8 weekly efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were associated with very small drops in eccentric hamstring strength, and efforts above 95% were too rare to show any relationship. Thresholds, outcomes, and populations differ, and no source tests this in returning athletes.

claims.text: In a case series of 100 male amateur and professional soccer players after ACL reconstruction, completing all five on-field rehabilitation stages almost prepared players for team training demands, but workloads stayed low compared with match play.

evidence.excerpt: A total of 100 male 11-a-side soccer players who were undergoing rehabilitation to return to competitive soccer after primary or secondary ACLR
Completion of all five OFR stages almost prepared them for team training demands; however, workloads remain low compared to match play.

claims.text: In the same case series, final-stage outputs relative to team training were 106% total distance, 104% high-intensity distance, 88% peak speed, 110% acceleration distance, and 48% deceleration distance, but relative to match play were 44%, 51%, 82%, 63%, and 26%.

evidence.excerpt: Typical external workload outputs in the final OFR stage aligned with team training demands for the total distance (TD) (106%), high-intensity distance (HID) (104%), peak speed (PS) (88%), acceleration distance (ACC) (110%), and deceleration distance (DEC) (48%)
but they were lower compared with match play demands (TD: 44%; HID: 51%; PS: 82%; ACC: 63%; and DEC: 26%).

claims.text: Citing earlier work, the case series authors describe on-field rehabilitation as the bridge between clinic-managed rehabilitation and the team-training environment with coaching and performance staff, and note that the published five-stage frameworks are based on expert opinion and single-case applications.

evidence.excerpt: OFR is thought to be the vital bridge between in-clinic medically managed rehabilitation and RTT environment with coaching/performance staff.
While both frameworks appear conceptually sound, they are based on expert opinion9,10,45 and single-case study46 applications.

claims.text: In the ACL case series, total distance plateaued after the early stages, and the authors suggest it is not a useful metric for return-to-competition decisions or for progressing through on-field rehabilitation.

evidence.excerpt: The plateau in TD suggests that it is not a useful metric for RTC decision-making or for progressing through OFR.

claims.text: In a single elite male soccer player after ACL reconstruction, peak running intensity in meters per minute during on-field rehabilitation could equal or exceed the player's own pre-injury team training and match values, but mechanical work per minute could not, and the authors note only drills such as 3v3 or 4v4 small-sided games are effective for overloading it.

evidence.excerpt: while typical team training and match m/min could be equated or even overloaded during the on-field rehabilitation (Upper panel), this was not the case for mechanical work

Peak intensity periods in terms of m/min (upper panel) and mechanical work/min (MW, lower panel) for the player when training collectively with the team before injury (n=33 sessions), during matches (n=8 matches), and during the on-field rehabilitation phase (n=31 sessions).

It is however often difficult to overload mechanical work/min at the session level (even with healthy players during team training) in comparison with match demands, and only some specific drills such as small-sided games with few players (i.e., 3v3 or 4v4) are effective for that

claims.text: The case study authors conclude that nothing replaces competition for performing some specific movements at high pace, such as cutting, decelerating, and ball interactions.

evidence.excerpt: This highlights the specificity of match demands and confirms that nothing replaces competition when it comes to performing some specific movements at a high pace (e.g., cutting, decelerating, ball interactions).

claims.text: The case study authors report that GPS-embedded inertial measurement units and analytics can monitor stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries during rehabilitation and can be used to guide phase progression.

evidence.excerpt: GPS-embed inertial measurement unit and associated analytics (e.g., ADI software) add invaluable sport-specific information to monitor stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries throughout the rehabilitation process, that can be used to guide phase progression

claims.text: The case study authors emphasize that late conditioning phases, though often seen as performance-staff led, require continuous and parallel collaboration within the multidisciplinary team.

evidence.excerpt: while these last conditioning phases of the return to sport process may be first seen as heavy performance staff-led (i.e., strength and conditioning, fitness coaches), we need to emphasize the continuous and parallel collaboration that is always required within the multidisciplinary team.

claims.text: In the ACL case with a hamstring graft, the authors, citing earlier work, describe hamstring strength as an important but not unique criterion for speed progression.

evidence.excerpt: especially in the case of a hamstring graft as in the present case
Hamstring strength is believed to be an important (but not unique) criterion for speed progression14

claims.text: In 18 elite sprinters with first-time hamstring strains, injured-leg strength and flexibility exceeded 90% of the uninjured leg at 6 weeks, but only 2 felt ready for maximal speed, so a 90% to 95% test criterion did not agree with the sprinters' own judgment.

evidence.excerpt: Eighteen elite sprinters with acute first-time hamstring strains were prospectively included in the study.

After 6 weeks, the performance of the injured leg in strength and flexibility tests exceeded 90% of that of the uninjured leg, but only 2 sprinters considered themselves ready to run at maximal speed.

Thus, a 90% to 95% level of test performance, as often is recommended as a criterion for full return to sports, was not in agreement with the sprinters’ own judgment that they could return safely to maximal speed running.

claims.text: In a survey of 62 physical therapists from elite Brazilian men's clubs managing hamstring strains, muscle strength (71%) and sprint or high-speed running performance (58%) were the only discharge criteria used by more than half, and the authors say the predictive value and cut-offs of such criteria need further study.

evidence.excerpt: This survey had 62 physical therapists from 35 of the 40 eligible clubs (87.5% representativeness).
Muscle strength levels (71%) and performance in sprints/high-speed running (58%) are the only outcomes used as criteria for discharge by more than half of respondents.
It is noteworthy that predictive value of such criteria for re-injury rate and its speciﬁc cut-offs for professional footballers require further investigation.

claims.text: The survey authors cite an expert Delphi consensus for return to play after hamstring strain in football that includes medical staff clearance, absence of pain on palpation and during strength, flexibility, and functional testing, similar hamstring flexibility, field-test performance, and psychological readiness.

evidence.excerpt: in which experts reached a consensus on the following criteria to support the RTP decision following HSI in football athletes: medical staff clearance, absence of pain on palpation, absence of pain during strength and ﬂexibility testing,
absence of pain during/after functional testing, similar hamstring ﬂexibility, performance on ﬁeld testing, and psychological readiness.

claims.text: Citing earlier work on the possible protective effect of sprint exposure, the survey authors consider including sprints in advanced rehabilitation phases advisable, and suggest that in some clubs other staff such as strength and conditioning coaches may be in charge of the transition to the field phase.

evidence.excerpt: Considering the potential preventive effect of the athletes' exposition to sprints on the risk of HSI (Edouard et al., 2023), the inclusion of this type of stimulus in more advanced phases of rehabilitation programs seems advisable.
It is possible, however, that other members of the health/coaching staff (e.g., strength and conditioning coaches) are in charge for the transition to the ﬁeld phase in some clubs.

claims.text: In retrospective data from 16 elite teams in top European leagues, there were no match hamstring injuries when exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed occurred two days before the match, while injuries still happened with no exposure or with exposures three or more days before; the authors state the observational design precludes causal conclusions.

evidence.excerpt: Retrospective data from 36 team-seasons (16 elite teams performing in top European leagues) were analyzed (627 players, 96 non-contact time loss match hamstring injuries).

Finally, irrespective of the turnaround length, there were no match hamstring injuries when > 95% MSS exposures occurred at D-2, while in contrast, injuries still happened when players were not exposed at all, or when these exposures occurred at D-3 and/or earlier within the turnaround.

While the present observational study design precludes the examination of causal relationships, the programming of > 95% MSS exposures at D-2 may help mitigate match hamstring injury occurrences in elite football.

claims.text: In 58 professional male soccer players observed over one and a half seasons, eccentric hamstring strength decreased when 7 to 8 weekly sprint efforts above 90% of maximum velocity were completed, with very small differences of 0.11% and 0.12% versus 0 to 2 and 5 to 6 efforts.

evidence.excerpt: Fifty-eight professional male footballers were observed over one-and-a-half seasons.
Eccentric hamstring strength levels significantly decrease when 7-8 weekly sprint efforts are completed at >90% of maximum velocity.
with significant differences occurring when comparing 7-8 sprint efforts with 0-2 efforts (0.11%, p = 0.03) and 5-6 efforts (0.12%, p = 0.03).

claims.text: In the ACL case series, deceleration distance reached 48% of training and 26% of match values while acceleration distance reached 110% and 63%, and the authors conclude players were underprepared for the deceleration demands of soccer after on-field rehabilitation.

evidence.excerpt: the DEC distance was markedly shorter than the ACC distance in our study (ACC: 110% of training and 63% of match play; DEC: 48% of training and 26% of match play), indicating that players are underprepared for the DEC demands of soccer after OFR.

claims.text: The case series authors state that on-field rehabilitation facilitated preparation for team training but did not fully prepare players for full team training workloads, highlighting the need for further training, such as modified training, before full team integration and return to competition.

evidence.excerpt: this study showed that OFR facilitates RTT preparation but does not fully prepare the players for the workload demands of full team training.
highlighting the need for further training (eg, modified training) before full integration with the team training practices and before RTC.

claims.text: In the hamstring strength study, players completed about one effort above 90% of maximum velocity per week on average, and weekly efforts above 95% showed no relationship with hamstring strength.

evidence.excerpt: in this study the players were found to complete, on average, approximately one effort per week
weekly efforts >95% of maximum velocity showed no relationship with hamstring strength

claims.text: In the return-to-train phase, the case study authors describe progressively introducing the player into team sessions while still managing his load, for example joining only some drills or playing small-sided games as a floater.

evidence.excerpt: This includes progressively introducing the player into team sessions while still managing his own load
the player takes only part in some but not all drills of the session, plays small-sided games but as a floater

claims.text: The hamstring strength study authors state that their study did not directly measure injury risk.

evidence.excerpt: Although it was established that eccentric hamstring strength is one of the risk factors in hamstring injury, this study did not directly measure injury risk.

claims.text: In the single ACL case, a step impulse asymmetry on return to running was associated with knee pain and required the player to stop running for a few days; on return and running on a softer pitch, both the pain and the asymmetry disappeared.

evidence.excerpt: This asymmetry was associated with reported right knee pain and required the player to stop running for a few days.
and while running on a softer pitch, both the pain and the asymmetry disappeared.

claims.text: In the ACL case series, transition between on-field stages was driven by comparing drills with how the knee and soft tissues responded to the loads, together with defined stage-specific criteria.

evidence.excerpt: The stage-to-stage transition was driven by a continuous comparison between different drills subjected to the player and the way the knee and soft tissues responded to the given loads along with defined stage-specific criteria.

claims.text: Surveyed physical therapists most often used pain (93.5%), muscle strength (89%), and function (85.5%) to progress hamstring rehabilitation, and the authors note that progression criteria are not consistent in the literature.

evidence.excerpt: The progression of athletes within rehabilitation programs is usually based on clinical and functional criteria, and the present study shows that pain (93.5%), muscle strength (89%) and functionality (85.5%) are the criteria most adopted.
In summary, the number of program phases and the progression criteria are not consistent in the literature.

claims.text: In the hamstring-graft ACL case, the team used isometric and eccentric strength benchmarks to guide running progression, for example above 70% isometric strength to run faster than 15 km/h and above 90% eccentric strength before near-maximal speeds and maximal changes of direction; the reference for these percentages is not stated.

evidence.excerpt: we used isometric and eccentric benchmarks to guide the run-based metabolic conditioning programming (e.g., >70% isometric strength to run >15 km/h
and >90% eccentric strength to reach speeds close to max and maximal change of direction intensities

claims.text: The case study authors recommend regularly monitoring fitness, range of motion, strength, and running mechanics during the season so practitioners have reference points to direct rehabilitation after injury.

evidence.excerpt: It is important to regularly monitor various indices of cardiovascular fitness, ROM, strength, and running mechanics during the season so that when an injury occurs, practitioners can have reference points toward which they can direct the rehabilitation process.

claims.text: The case series authors note that pre-injury peak speed data were lacking in most cases, so only absolute values were reported.

evidence.excerpt: The lack of preinjury PS data in most cases led to reporting only absolute values.

claims.text: In the ACL case series, the 33% of players who reached the final on-field stage had higher return-to-competition rates than the rest (90% vs 71%), but the authors say it is unclear whether the workloads, level of play, or number of sessions explained this.

evidence.excerpt: Players who reached stage 5 of the OFR program (33%) had higher RTC rates compared with the rest of the cohort (90% vs 71%; P = .016).

it remains unclear whether increased OFR workloads enhanced physical and psychological readiness for RTC or whether it was the level of play or the number of OFR sessions that determined higher RTC rates.

claims.text: In 4 to 8 day turnarounds pooled, exposures above 95% of maximal sprinting speed two days before a match occurred in 480 player-turnarounds with 0 match hamstring injuries, compared with 2 injuries in 215 at one day before and 46 injuries in 11,168 with no exposure.

evidence.excerpt: at D-2, n = 480 and 0 injuries; at D-1, n = 215 and 2 injuries, and no exposure throughout the turnaround, n = 11168 and 46 injuries.

assumptions: The injury type is not specified, so ACL reconstruction and hamstring strain evidence is used only as indirect support for end-stage field progression.
The athlete's current phase is treated as comparable to the late on-field rehabilitation and return-to-train phases described in the sources.
GPS or similar field tracking is assumed to be available to staff for monitoring field outputs.
coverageGaps: No study tests a structured 7 to 10 day end-stage progression or explicit progress, hold, or regress rules.
No collegiate field-sport athletes, and no female field-sport athletes, in the end stage of return to sport.
No validated cut-offs or composite criteria that predict reinjury after unrestricted return.
No evidence comparing decision-ownership models between rehabilitation and performance staff.

No direct evidence on adapting staged exposure for a returning athlete when practice opportunities are limited during a competition schedule; related evidence on turnaround timing and players with little match time comes from uninjured squads.
A controlled or prospective study in collegiate field-sport athletes that tests a structured end-stage progression with explicit progress, hold, or regress rules.
